item.title: The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season
item.description: Super Typhoon In-fa developed an unusually large eye, and the remnants of Typhoon Champi transitioned into an extratropical storm that targeted Alaska.

item.title: Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can tackle several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. Already tested for initial safety in humans, the experimental treatment could offer a faster path toward therapies that target the disease at its roots.

item.title: Large Hadron Collider reveals evidence of Big Bang matter in surprisingly small collisions
item.description: Scientists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider have uncovered compelling new evidence that even relatively small atomic collisions can recreate the extraordinary state of matter that filled the universe moments after the Big Bang. Known as quark-gluon plasma, this exotic substance forms at temperatures more than 100,000 times hotter than the center of the Sun, causing ordinary particles to break apart into their fundamental building blocks.

item.title: Scientists just found a loophole that could let black holes split in two
item.description: Scientists have discovered a possible loophole in the laws that normally prevent black holes from splitting apart, suggesting that extremely fast-spinning black holes might divide into two. The surprising finding raises the possibility of an entirely new black hole phenomenon that future telescopes could potentially detect.

item.title: Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half
item.description: A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps liver cells remove harmful substances from the bloodstream.

One major trial failed to show a benefit, and now scientists are scrambling to work out what that means.

item.title: NASA’s Hubble Uncovers Case of Missing Oxygen in Nearby Dwarf Galaxies
item.description: NASA’s Hubble studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies and found that much of the oxygen they expected to see is missing.

item.title: Extra weight may be aging your brain faster than you think
item.description: A major 24-year study involving more than 8,200 adults suggests that excess body weight may accelerate brain aging, leading to faster declines in memory, concentration, and decision-making skills. The connection was particularly strong among people over 65, raising concerns about the long-term effects of obesity on brain health.

item.title: IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos
item.description: Mysterious particles called neutrinos constantly stream through our bodies, and scientists are now detecting incredibly powerful versions arriving from distant cosmic sources using a massive observatory buried in Antarctic ice. These elusive “ghost particles” could hold extraordinary clues about the Big Bang, extreme cosmic events, and some of the universe’s greatest mysteries.

item.title: Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation
item.description: Scientists are calling for a major rethink of how we manage high blood pressure, suggesting that eating more potassium could be just as important as cutting back on salt. A new report finds that combining increased potassium intake with reduced sodium consumption may offer greater benefits for blood pressure control than sodium reduction alone.

item.title: New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss
item.description: Researchers have developed a remarkable new electronic implant that could transform type 2 diabetes treatment by lowering blood sugar without insulin or traditional drugs. The device uses a special electrically powered catalyst to convert excess glucose into a substance that the body eliminates through urine, potentially preventing unwanted energy from being stored as fat. In diabetic mice, the implant precisely controlled blood sugar and promoted weight loss.

item.title: Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice
item.description: In a surprising discovery, scientists found that certain diets associated with obesity can make cancer immunotherapy more effective in mice, challenging traditional assumptions about diet and cancer treatment. The findings suggest that the secret may lie in how food interacts with gut bacteria to strengthen the immune system's response to cancer.

item.title: NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover breaks historic record after traveling 28 miles
item.description: NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a historic record by traveling 28.10 miles across Mars, farther than any vehicle has ever driven on another world. Armed with groundbreaking autonomous navigation technology and increasingly advanced driving capabilities, the rover is pushing the boundaries of robotic exploration.

item.title: NASA reveals a haunting skull hidden in Antarctica’s ice
item.description: NASA satellites have captured an eerie, skull-shaped formation on a remote Antarctic island, but its haunting appearance conceals a troubling warning about melting glaciers. Unusually warm winter temperatures have exposed large areas of dark ice, potentially accelerating future melting and gradually transforming the skull's ghostly features.

item.title: 30,000-year-old DNA reveals Ice Age Europeans were far more connected than we thought
item.description: Scientists have uncovered surprising DNA evidence that Europeans living more than 30,000 years ago were connected across vast distances, challenging the idea that ancient populations remained largely isolated. Genetic clues from human remains and cave sediments reveal prehistoric migration, long-lasting communities, and survival through the harshest conditions of the Ice Age.

item.title: Pennsylvania’s Grand Canyon
item.description: Amid the warm hues of fall foliage, Pine Creek Gorge forms a deep scar in the Allegheny Plateau.

item.title: Even moderate drinking linked to cancer and early death, major study finds
item.description: A major new study challenges the idea that moderate drinking is safe, finding that even relatively small amounts of alcohol increase the risk of cancer, heart disease, and premature death. Researchers found no overall health benefits from drinking and warn that consuming more than one alcoholic beverage per day can significantly increase long-term health risks.

item.title: NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past
item.description: NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have uncovered surprising clues about the solar system’s origins by studying 27 tiny, distant objects beyond Neptune. Scientists discovered that these ancient building blocks of planets have remained remarkably unchanged for billions of years, while their unexpected sizes and numbers challenge existing theories of planet formation.

item.title: Scientists find surprisingly little evidence that medical cannabis helps you sleep
item.description: A major new review challenges the growing enthusiasm for medical cannabis as an insomnia treatment, finding little reliable evidence that it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or daytime functioning. Researchers caution that this doesn't mean cannabis is ineffective, only that existing studies are too weak to establish whether it works.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03485-2 Start-up founders routinely talk about their failed companies. Academia could learn from them, says Mary Ryan.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03346-y Pressures due to the continuing US–Iran conflict are mounting as early-career researchers endure frozen immigration status, employment limbo and families caught in the war.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03511-3 From rodents to humans, tools that enable large-scale, single-cell neuronal recordings are exposing the inner workings of the brain.

item.title: In Indonesia, PhD students blow the whistle on bad supervision
item.description: Nature, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02465-w The nation plans to boost the number of doctoral candidates, but some early-career researchers warn of systemic challenges, including poor-quality supervision.

item.title: How researchers debunked ‘race science’: ‘a triumph of scientific self-correction’
item.description: Nature, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03507-z An account of how nineteenth-century studies aiming to find a biological basis for human races were dismantled by good scientific practices — although their effects are still felt today.

item.title: ‘A perfect scientist, a perfect mum’: researchers mourn two biologists’ deaths in Spanish train crash
item.description: Nature, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03564-4 Scientists pay tribute to Marta Shahbazi Alonso and Tamara González Costa who died on their way to a developmental-biology meeting.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day
item.description: A surprising new study suggests that eating peanuts every day could help support brain health and memory in older adults. Researchers found that consuming about two servings of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for 16 weeks improved insulin responsiveness in brain regions important for memory, a function that often weakens with age and has been linked to Alzheimer's disease.

item.title: Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease
item.description: A UCLA study found that long-term exposure to a common pesticide was linked to more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease. Scientists also uncovered how the chemical damages brain cells and identified a promising way to protect them.

item.title: Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule
item.description: Scientists have built a groundbreaking molecular motor that spins in either direction using electricity, inspired by a machine invented more than 2,000 years ago. Even more remarkably, its rotation can boost electrical conductivity by up to 100 times, potentially transforming the future of molecular electronics.

item.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
item.description: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

item.title: Drinking tea may help protect your heart, but there’s a surprising catch
item.description: A massive study of nearly 486,000 adults found that regularly drinking tea was associated with an 11% lower risk of heart and blood vessel diseases. The lowest risk was linked to drinking roughly six to eight cups per day, with black tea showing more consistent benefits than green tea.

item.title: Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer
item.description: Scientists at the University of Virginia have developed a promising new strategy to fight glioblastoma, one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat forms of brain cancer. Their experimental approach combines focused ultrasound, tiny nanoparticles, and genetic molecules called microRNAs to attack multiple cancer-driving genes simultaneously.

item.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
item.description: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

item.title: Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
item.description: A mysterious particle overlooked for decades may hold the key to why matter survived the Big Bang, allowing stars, planets, and life to exist. Scientists believe this forgotten neutrino reshaped the early universe and may have left detectable gravitational wave signals that could help unlock the cosmos’s deepest mysteries.

item.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
item.description: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden driver of high cholesterol and a way to stop it
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a hidden mechanism that allows high-cholesterol diets to undermine the body's natural cholesterol defenses, and blocking it dramatically lowered harmful LDL cholesterol in mice. Even more promising, an experimental drug targeting this pathway has already passed an early human safety trial, potentially speeding the development of a new treatment for high cholesterol.

item.title: Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer
item.description: Scientists at Johns Hopkins have uncovered a crucial missing link between a common gut bacterium and colorectal cancer, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for nearly two decades. The bacterium, Bacteroides fragilis, produces a toxin that damages the colon’s protective lining, triggers chronic inflammation, and promotes tumor formation.

item.title: A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
item.description: A remarkable 4,000-year-old defensive structure discovered in Morocco is rewriting what scientists thought they knew about ancient North African civilizations. The massive fortifications reveal unexpectedly sophisticated prehistoric societies and suggest that the region played a much greater role in Mediterranean history than previously recognized.

item.title: Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424°F
item.description: Scientists have discovered a surprising mechanism that allows certain metals to resist cracking at temperatures as low as -253°C (-424°F), when similar materials typically become dangerously brittle. Instead of breaking, two experimental alloys reorganize their internal structures, creating new ways to absorb stress and remain flexible.

item.title: 75,000-year-old Neanderthal may have been killed by a spear aimed at the heart
item.description: A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been killed by a wooden spear deliberately aimed at the heart, revealing rare evidence of prehistoric violence. A circular hole in the shoulder blade suggests the weapon pierced the chest and caused a rapidly fatal injury. Surprisingly, the same individual had survived an earlier devastating facial injury, suggesting other Neanderthals provided care and support.

item.title: Scientists discover a bacterial defense so strange they thought it was broken
item.description: Scientists have discovered a bizarre bacterial defense system that works almost completely backward from anything seen before. Unlike typical bacterial immune systems that keep a deadly toxin under control until a virus attacks, this unusual mechanism waits until an infection begins before producing the DNA that switches on its lethal weapon. The infected bacterium then destroys itself, preventing the virus from multiplying and spreading to neighboring cells.

item.title: A surprising vitamin A discovery is changing what scientists know about vision
item.description: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising process that helps humans develop sharp vision before birth, challenging decades of assumptions about how the eye forms. Using miniature human retinas grown in the lab, researchers discovered that a vitamin A derivative and thyroid hormones work together to shape the foveola, the tiny region at the center of the retina responsible for our sharpest vision.

item.title: Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang
item.description: Scientists have recreated a primordial state of matter from the dawn of the universe by colliding oxygen nuclei at nearly the speed of light. The surprising results show that this exotic substance can form in smaller, lower-energy collisions than previously demonstrated, challenging the known boundaries of early-universe physics.

item.title: A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
item.description: A major international study found that a simple blood test could help predict Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline years before symptoms appear, with the highest-risk individuals facing a 38% chance of impairment within five years and an estimated 78% chance within 10 years. Scientists believe the discovery could pave the way for earlier intervention and future treatments designed to prevent Alzheimer’s before memory problems begin.

item.title: Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months
item.description: A promising new study suggests that more than half of younger adults with type 2 diabetes could achieve remission in just six months through a combination of a low-calorie diet and structured exercise. Researchers found that 54% of participants under age 45 who followed an intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission, compared with just 4% receiving usual care.

item.title: Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
item.description: Scientists have created a miniature universe in the laboratory that could help answer one of the biggest mysteries in physics: What is time, and where does it come from? Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. Remarkably, the experiment showed that time could emerge from changes happening inside the system, without relying on an external clock.

item.title: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
item.description: Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.

item.title: A computer scientist breaks through a limit that stood since 1996
item.description: A computer scientist has achieved a breakthrough in a nearly 25-year-old problem involving how computers calculate distances across enormous networks. The new algorithm delivers more reliable estimates for closely connected points without sacrificing speed, overcoming a longstanding limitation of earlier methods. Its secret lies in a smarter way of sampling network connections at multiple scales.

item.title: Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
item.description: A surprising discovery by astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from a dense fog of hydrogen roughly 13 billion years ago. Scientists once believed powerful winds from exploding stars helped radiation escape galaxies and clear that cosmic fog, but new observations reveal that these winds actually block radiation instead.

item.title: Scientists reveal a hidden snakebite crisis killing up to 513,000 people a year
item.description: A startling new study suggests that venomous snakebites are killing far more people worldwide than official statistics indicate, with an estimated 274,000 to 513,000 deaths every year. Researchers found that as many as 7 million people could suffer snake envenoming annually, while more than 800,000 survivors are left with long-term disabilities.

item.title: Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly
item.description: Scientists have uncovered hidden aggressive cancer cells in children whose tumors were previously considered lower risk, revealing why some cases of rhabdomyosarcoma become unexpectedly deadly. The discovery could help doctors identify dangerous tumors earlier and develop personalized treatments that improve survival while reducing unnecessary chemotherapy.

item.title: Astronauts just gave the International Space Station a powerful upgrade
item.description: Two astronauts completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk to install a new solar array on the International Space Station, bringing NASA one step closer to a major power upgrade. Once the final array is installed on November 5, the station will have up to 30% more available power, supporting critical operations and its eventual controlled deorbit.

item.title: Scientists confirm global warming is accelerating faster than ever recorded
item.description: Earth is warming faster than ever recorded, with scientists detecting a major acceleration in global temperatures since around 2015. A new study reveals that the warming rate has surged to approximately 0.35°C per decade, nearly double the average pace observed from 1970 to 2015. After removing natural climate fluctuations, researchers confirmed the acceleration with more than 98% statistical confidence.

item.title: A mysterious star system just 16 light-years away may be hiding habitable planets
item.description: Astronomers have solved a 170-year-old planetary mystery in a nearby two-star system, discovering that a mysterious wobble was caused by stellar activity rather than a giant planet. Although Jupiter-sized worlds have been ruled out in key regions, smaller, potentially habitable planets could still be waiting to be discovered just 16 light-years from Earth.

item.title: Scientists discover mysterious seahorse lookalikes that no one has ever seen alive
item.description: Scientists have discovered that three bizarre deep-sea fish that look exactly like seahorses actually belong to a separate evolutionary group, proving that nature created the same unusual body shape more than once. Nicknamed "sea muppets," these elusive creatures are known from just seven specimens, and no one has ever seen one alive.

item.title: Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal
item.description: A surprising discovery at UC San Diego suggests that chronic lower back pain may become deeply embedded in the brain's sense of personal identity. Researchers found that movement-triggered pain activates a brain network associated with self-awareness and memories, even though ordinary acute pain typically shuts this network down. This unexpected difference could explain why conventional pain medications often provide limited relief and why fear, anticipation, and past experiences can intensify chronic pain.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03455-8 Announcement by IEEE follows publication of a study showing the retracted papers are linked to paper mills.

item.title: Are dinosaur fossils hogging top journals? Analysis sparks debate over ‘charismatic’ finds
item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03512-2 Fossils of dinosaurs, mammals and other glamorous species are over-represented in high-profile titles, suggests a study of thousands of palaeontology papers.

item.title: A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms
item.description: Scientists have identified a weakened brain signal that may connect several seemingly unrelated symptoms of schizophrenia, including sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity. The surprising discovery could help explain the disorder's underlying mechanisms and potentially lead to earlier detection and new treatments.

item.title: Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
item.description: A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not established.

item.title: A 700,000-year-old elephant tooth reveals a lost world where early humans lived
item.description: A remarkably preserved elephant tooth dating back nearly 700,000 years has revealed a surprisingly lush prehistoric world where giant elephants and early humans lived side by side. Discovered in northern Israel alongside ancient stone tools, the tooth belonged to a straight-tusked elephant, one of the largest land mammals of the Ice Age.

item.title: NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s
item.description: NASA’s Juno spacecraft has discovered that Jupiter uses a surprisingly complex system of powerful plasma waves and multiple shock regions to defend against the solar wind. The findings reveal major differences between Jupiter and Earth and could help scientists understand the enormous shock waves produced by exploding stars.

item.title: Einstein's equations may explain the universe without dark energy
item.description: Mathematicians have uncovered what they argue is a fundamental flaw in the standard model of the universe, potentially challenging the need for dark energy. Their calculations suggest that the mathematical framework used to describe cosmic expansion is inherently unstable and that the universe could accelerate naturally under Einstein's original theory of gravity. The findings also raise surprising questions about whether our location in the universe is as ordinary as scientists have long assumed.

item.title: Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
item.description: Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.

item.title: Scientists discover that cranberry juice may help fight tooth decay
item.description: Cranberry juice may offer an unexpected benefit beyond its reputation for helping prevent urinary tract infections: protecting teeth from decay. Researchers at the University of Illinois Chicago discovered that pure, unsweetened cranberry juice slowed the regrowth of dental plaque bacteria and reduced their production of acids that damage tooth enamel. The secret may lie in naturally occurring compounds called proanthocyanidins, which interfere with harmful bacteria.

item.title: 128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history
item.description: Ancient ice discovered high in Tibet may be more than 128,000 years old, preserving an extraordinary record of Earth's climate that scientists previously thought had been lost. The discovery reveals a rare glimpse into the last ice age and could reshape our understanding of how glaciers survive dramatic changes in global climate.

item.title: Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal
item.description: Researchers have discovered a small group of brain cells that prevents dangerous blood pressure swings, even when average readings appear normal. The finding reveals a hidden source of cardiovascular risk and could open the door to new treatments that protect the heart and brain.

item.title: Scientists just broke a textbook rule of physics
item.description: Scientists have defied a long-standing rule of laser physics by generating X-rays with much higher energies than conventional theory predicts. The surprising discovery reveals how two electrons working together can overcome a previously accepted limit, opening new possibilities for quantum research.

item.title: Meteors don't just burn up. What really happens is far more violent
item.description: Scientists have uncovered seven surprising stages that space rocks go through as they hurtle toward Earth, revealing that melting and violent fragmentation, rather than simple evaporation, determine their fate. The discovery could help explain why meteorites scatter across the ground and how dangerous asteroids explode in Earth's atmosphere.

item.title: Even stupendous black holes can’t explain dark matter
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03386-4 The theoretical objects would have left a larger imprint on cosmic radiation if they were a source of the invisible force pulling together the galaxies.

item.title: Daily briefing: The three red flags of suspicious journals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03548-4 These warning signs suggest a journal might be engaging in dubious publishing activities. Plus, the brain clears out faulty neurons at birth and whether a giant ‘sunshade’ could cool Earth.

item.title: How the US mid-term elections could shake up science
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03479-0 A Democratic victory in Congress could halt the Trump administration’s controversial grant-review plan and curb some of its funding actions.

item.title: A single sauna session sends immune cells surging through your body
item.description: A new Finnish study reveals that just 30 minutes in a sauna can temporarily flood the bloodstream with additional white blood cells, potentially helping the immune system patrol the body and detect threats. The surprising response resembles the immune boost seen during exercise and may help explain some of the health benefits linked to sauna bathing.

item.title: Smaller EV batteries, longer range? Scientists may have found a way
item.description: Scientists have developed a new technology that could make electric vehicle batteries smaller, lighter, and longer-lasting, potentially allowing cars to travel farther on a single charge. By borrowing precision manufacturing techniques from computer chip production, they found a way to prevent damaging lithium buildup that has held back next-generation batteries.

item.title: A simple daily fiber supplement reduced arthritis pain and improved strength
item.description: A new clinical trial suggests that a simple daily fiber supplement could significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis pain, improve muscle strength, and make the body less sensitive to pain. Researchers discovered that the benefits may be linked to changes in gut bacteria and the hormone GLP-1, revealing a promising new approach to arthritis relief.

item.title: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
item.description: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people have difficulty recognizing faces and reading emotions.

item.title: Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11348-z Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions

item.title: Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11335-4 Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination

item.title: Why did ancient humans avoid this lush paradise
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03486-1 A new expedition into the Rub’ al Khali desert finds no evidence of ancient human settlement.

item.title: This Arabian desert was once a lush paradise. Why did ancient humans avoid it?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03484-3 Expedition revealed that water wasn’t enough for human settlement — plus, proposals to block sunlight get serious.

item.title: Accounting of Africa’s water reveals a management gap
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03260-3 A map of Africa’s water demand reveals that the scarcity of water is only part of the problem facing the continent — management is a separate challenge.

item.title: The brain liquidates billions of mutant neurons around the time we’re born
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03444-x Faulty neurons can contribute to various neurological conditions, but researchers have uncovered a system that might clean them up.

item.title: Daily briefing: The big push to personalize psychiatry
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03531-z A data-driven approach could match treatments to individuals with more precision. Plus, funders in Europe are backing preprint-led publishing and whether professors should care about student evaluations.

item.title: Tethered to stone: how rock and water availability shaped early desert occupation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03263-0 Fresh water in deserts often points to sites with signs of early humans and stone tools. But, in Arabia’s Rub’ al Khali region, water alone does not predict occupation.

item.title: What students think about my teaching doesn’t matter. Am I wrong?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02202-3 A jury weighs in on whether teaching assessments are popularity contests or an important tool.

item.title: How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03402-7 Fresh ideas are welcome in a discipline in which progress is rare — provided they are applied rigorously.

item.title: Lactate takes a shortcut into mitochondria to power the heart
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03261-2 A cellular fuel called lactate is channelled directly into energy-generating organelles in heart muscle, defying the prevailing view about lactate transport.

item.title: Clues about complex life come from freshly cultivated archaea
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03294-7 Two archaeal strains that belong to a lineage closely related to the ancestor of eukaryotic cells (complex cells with membrane-bound organelles) have been brought into culture. Their simple internal organization, elaborate surface structures, microbial partnerships and protein-dependent lifestyle provide clues about how eukaryotic cells arose.

item.title: Preprint-centric publishing model gets major boost
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03445-w European funders put weight behind emerging ‘publish, review, curate’ approach for preprints.

item.title: These three red flags could unmask dodgy journals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03325-3 As poor publishing practices proliferate, scholarly databases are under pressure to ensure the titles they list are reputable.

item.title: Is research funding now a lottery? Elite funder ERC swamped by applications
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03476-3 A marked rise in submissions for the European Research Council’s grants is pushing down success rates.

item.title: Dengue comes back even in vaccinated people — new clues
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03488-z Researchers help to answer a question dogging the development of improved vaccines against the mosquito-borne disease.

item.title: The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03391-7 Could a blood sample, a brain scan and a look at your phone data transform how your psychiatrist treats you?

item.title: Could a giant sunshade in space ‘solve global warming’? Scientists are taking the idea seriously
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03415-2 Some say the concept is complete fantasy, but a detailed analysis suggests that the falling cost of rocket launches might make it feasible in a few decades.

item.title: An unexpected function of a cell-cycle enzyme might explain the toxic effects of its inhibitors
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03288-5 A previously unknown mechanism required for cells to start proliferating has been identified. A combination of mathematical modelling and cell-based experiments shows that the enzyme WEE1 switches off a protein-degradation complex to allow cell proliferation to start, with implications for WEE1 inhibitors currently in trials for cancer treatments.

item.title: Meta-study sparks questions about what it means to be good at regulating emotions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03262-1 A first-of-its kind consortium reveals a lack of correlation between behavioural and neural measures of a person’s emotional regulation.

item.title: How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03248-z The largest analysis of its kind reveals the public’s changing relationship with science and the people who do it.

item.title: Genetic variants that alter gene regulation in specific cell types are closely tied to disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03067-2 Single-cell profiling of nearly 2,000 people brings scientists closer to understanding the link between genetic variation, gene expression and health.

item.title: Ribbon made of carbon pentagons and heptagons has metallic properties
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03298-3 Ribbons that are composed exclusively of five- and seven-carbon rings have metal-like electron transport and conductance. The ribbons can be synthesized by linking previously inaccessible chains of paired five-membered rings, providing a route to making highly conducting carbon nanoribbons.

item.title: Where have all the saucers flown?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03107-x Missed encounters.

item.title: The shifting sands of research independence: why mid-career scientists crave security
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02670-7 A project to improve understanding of an often-neglected group in academia aims to help its members to navigate career uncertainty.

item.title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11180-5 A geoarchaeological survey of the Rub’ al Khali (the Empty Quarter of Arabia) and spatial modelling of the Arabian Peninsula suggest that human settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and stone suitable for making tools, rather than water alone.

item.title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11211-1 A subset of necrotizing enterocolitis in infants is mediated specifically by the Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin.

item.title: Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10438-2 Whole-genome sequencing and cell-level gene expression measurements show that length variation in tandem repeats in the human genome contributes to cell type-specific differences in gene regulation and expression, as well as the architecture of complex traits.

item.title: Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11223-x Pseudo-direct bandgap character in bismuth sulfide retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination while preserving strong light absorption.

item.title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11190-3 Single-neuron sequencing shows that widespread genomic abnormalities are common prenatally but largely eliminated around birth, indicating developmental genome quality control in human neurons.

item.title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11195-y Computational simulations of a neural network based on fly connectomes identify a three-neuron circuit that is organized to produce leg motor rhythms for walking.

item.title: Narrow carbon pentaheptite nanoribbon as a covalent metal
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11202-2 Planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons are synthesized by laterally fusing polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains, suggesting a possible route towards carbon quantum wires.

item.title: Molecular underpinnings of rheumatic diseases and emerging therapeutic concepts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10966-x Improved molecular insights into inflammatory rheumatic diseases are enabling better disease control and advancing the field towards achieving durable remission and eventual cure.

item.title: Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11214-y An experimental concept enabling attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone is demonstrated and used to visualize the lightwave-driven electron motion of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene.

item.title: Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11181-4 Dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory.

item.title: T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11219-7 In systemic lupus erythematosus, aberrant splicing in neutrophils generates novel peptides that are presented on MHC I, driving CD4+ and CD8+ T cell activation, clonal expansion and IgG autoantibody responses, establishing neoantigen-driven autoimmune immunity.

item.title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10721-2 Phase 1 of TenK10K takes single-cell RNA sequencing and matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals, enabling detection of associations for common and rare genetic variants, the latter of which have been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression.

item.title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11203-1 Sensorimotor and amygdala activation, but not canonical prefrontal control circuits, indicate emotion regulation capacity.

item.title: Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11208-w Tumour assembloids, which model components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts and tumour-infiltrating immune cells, are used to identify an essential pathway that mediates heterogeneous therapeutic responses.

item.title: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11182-3 In mouse myocardium, glucose oxidation persists in the absence of the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, with mitochondrial MCT1 importing lactate into mitochondria and LDHB oxidizing it to pyruvate and NADH, sustaining cardiac energetics and preventing stress-induced heart failure.

item.title: Eukaryotes’ closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11170-7 Cultures reveal conservation of cell structure, physical symbioses and anaerobiosis across Heimdallarchaeia (the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes) and other Promethearchaeota.

item.title: Monolithically and in situ integrated PbS infrared imagers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11222-y A method for growing infrared image sensors directly from solution using raw materials by monolithic in situ integration of high-performance semiconductor PbS photodetectors on readout integrated circuits is described, yielding films with excellent electronic properties.

item.title: Time-reversal-symmetry-breaking spin injection from a compensated magnet
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11227-7 Experiments show that altermagnetic Mn5Si3 generates spin currents despite zero net magnetization, demonstrating a central prediction of altermagnetic spintronics.

item.title: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11147-6 A triplet carbene molecule in a tailored crystal provides a stable single-molecule spin–photon interface with millisecond coherence, advancing chemically engineered molecular qubits for quantum networking.
